children.label: The Gap Between Demo and Deployment

children.value: Over the past weeks, we’ve built increasingly sophisticated AI systems:
: Type-safe agents with PydanticAI, tool use, evaluations
: MCP servers, distributed tools, security fundamentals
—code that demonstrates concepts and works on your laptop.
But there’s a significant gap between “it works” and “it works reliably for thousands of users.”
Must work on all machines, always
This lecture bridges that gap—covering the essential patterns for production, safety considerations that matter, and where the field is heading.
When deploying agent systems at scale, you’ll encounter three main patterns:
User → API → Agent → LLM → Agent → API → User
Simple to implement, easy to reason about
Use when: Response time < 30 seconds (chatbots, Q&A)

User → API → Queue → Workers → LLM
     ← Task ID ←
User → Poll Status → Database
User gets task ID immediately, polls for results
Use when: Tasks take > 30 seconds (document analysis, batch processing)
Event Source → Message Bus → Multiple Agents listening
Use when: Multiple systems need to react to same data (trading, monitoring)
: Event-driven architecture mirrors information diffusion in social networks—events propagate through connected components.
LLM APIs fail. Not often, but enough to matter:
Without protection, your system keeps hammering a failing service, making things worse.
: Too many failures, block requests immediately (fail fast)
: After timeout, test if service recovered
: This is a reputation system! The API builds reputation through success, loses it through failures. The circuit breaker is the enforcement mechanism.
You can’t improve what you can’t measure. Production AI systems need:
Request rate, error rate, latency (P50, P95, P99)
Tool call accuracy (% of valid calls)
: Instrument everything, analyze regularly, optimize iteratively.
GitHub Copilot is one of the most successful AI agent deployments:
: Millions of users, billions of completions
: 55% acceptance rate (remarkably high for AI suggestions)
: Use multiple LLM providers, route based on availability and cost, fallback if primary fails
: Cache common completions, use semantic similarity for cache hits → 40% cost reduction
: Show tokens as generated, user sees progress immediately, can cancel slow completions
: Simple completions → fast small model, complex refactoring → larger model
: Track acceptance rate, A/B test prompts and models, continuous improvement
: Production AI isn’t just about making it work—it’s about making it work reliably, affordably, and measurably.
Suppose you deploy an AI agent that helps customers with financial advice.

: It systematically recommends riskier investments to older users. Why? It learned from historical data where younger clients complained more. The optimization objective (maximize satisfaction scores) rewarded this behavior.
Nothing wrong with the code. Everything wrong with the incentives.
: ensuring AI systems pursue the goals we actually want, not just the objectives we can easily measure.
: “When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.”
: We can only optimize for what we can measure, but what we can measure often doesn’t capture what we actually value.
We specify an objective, but it doesn’t capture what we want
Example: “Maximize customer satisfaction” → give everyone free refunds
System finds unintended ways to maximize reward
Example: RL agent in boat race spins in circles collecting bonus points instead of finishing
From game theory: deception can be rational if hard to detect and there’s no reputation cost
Example: Poker AI learns to bluff without being taught
System fails when deployed in contexts different from training
Example: Model trained on US data fails on international users
. How do we create incentives that align AI behavior with human values? This is the principal-agent problem we studied in Week 9—but with AI as the agent.
embed principles directly into the system
: Have the model evaluate its own response against the constitution
: Model improves response based on critique

1. Be helpful, harmless, and honest
2. Respect user privacy and data protection
3. Avoid bias and discrimination
4. Be transparent about limitations and uncertainty
5. Defer to humans for high-stakes decisions
6. Refuse harmful requests
Makes values explicit rather than implicit
Creates a repeated game with self-monitoring
: This mirrors how communities enforce cooperation—define standards, monitor behavior, sanction violations. The constitution becomes self-enforcing.
: Even without training, you can use constitutional prompting—include principles in your system prompt and ask the model to verify compliance before responding.
The EU AI Act (2024) is the most comprehensive AI regulation to date. It uses a
Social scoring, manipulation of vulnerable people
Strict requirements: risk management, documentation, human oversight, transparency
: Up to €35M or 7% of global revenue.
If building AI for employment, healthcare, or similar domains → expect significant compliance requirements
Even “limited risk” systems need transparency (users must know they’re talking to AI)
Document everything: architecture, data, testing, decisions
Optimal regulation balances these, but the optimum is uncertain
When building AI agent systems, work through this checklist:
What objectives are we optimizing? Are they aligned with actual goals?
Who could be harmed? How do we mitigate?
Least privilege (tools only have necessary permissions)
Test for bias across demographic groups
Evaluation metrics that match actual goals
: Safety isn’t a feature you add at the end. It’s a property of the entire system design.
Let’s step back and see the arc of this course:
: Simple structures (nodes, edges) create emergent properties (small-world effect, clustering, centrality).
: Simple rules (“move if unhappy”) create emergent outcomes (segregation, wealth inequality).
: Strategic interaction leads to equilibria. Mechanism design shapes incentives.
: Learning agents with tools, memory, and reasoning. Multi-agent systems and swarms.
: How do individual components create collective behavior?
—understanding systems where the whole is more than the sum of parts.
AI agents are the newest and most powerful components we can add to these systems. They reason, adapt, and coordinate in ways that simple rule-based agents cannot.

: Beyond text to vision, audio, and action. AI agents that “see” spatial patterns, have voice conversations, interact with physical/digital worlds. Research opportunity: How do multimodal capabilities change emergent behavior in agent swarms?

: Current LLMs forget after their context window fills. Emerging solutions include infinite context windows, external memory systems (vector databases, knowledge graphs), and semantic compression. Research opportunity: How does memory duration affect equilibrium strategies in repeated games?

: Models that learn representations working across text, vision, code, and actions. The goal: agents that reason about interventions and counterfactuals, not just correlations. Research opportunity: Can AI trained on game theory transfer knowledge to predict human market behavior?

: Current frontier models require enormous compute. But efficiency is improving rapidly—smaller models matching larger ones through better training. The thermodynamic limits of computation will eventually matter, pushing toward neuromorphic and quantum approaches.
The field is young. Many fundamental questions remain open—questions you could work on.
1. Emergent Behavior in AI Agent Swarms
We know simple rule-based agents create emergence (Schelling model). What happens with intelligent agents?
What patterns emerge in large AI agent populations?
How does network topology affect AI swarm behavior?
Can we predict emergent properties from agent designs?
Classical game theory assumes perfect rationality. LLMs don’t compute Nash equilibria explicitly.
Do LLMs converge to Nash equilibria with experience?
How does prompt framing affect strategic behavior?
What happens in complex games (auctions, negotiation, coalition formation)?
How should we design markets for AI agents?
Which mechanisms work well when participants are AI?
How do we prevent AI agents from gaming mechanisms?
What market structures optimize for AI services?
Traditional ABMs use simple rules. What if some agents are AI-driven?
How do intelligent agents change system dynamics?
Your computational social science training equips you to tackle these questions.
The future isn’t humans vs. AI or AI replacing humans. It’s
: Human leads, AI assists (GitHub Copilot, research assistants)
: AI provides specialized knowledge, human decides (medical diagnosis support)
: Human and AI iterate together (data analysis, writing)
: Human sets goals, AI executes, human reviews (automated trading)
: Human-AI collaboration is a cooperative game. The mechanism design question: how do we align incentives so AI acts in human interest?
: Learning how to work effectively with AI. This is increasingly valuable—and you’ve been developing it throughout this course.
Computational social science + AI skills open many paths:
: PhD programs in CS, Economics, Sociology, Information Science. Research in computational social science, multi-agent systems, AI safety.
: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind. Roles in safety research, alignment, policy analysis. Your advantage: understanding AI in social/economic context.
: Microsoft, Amazon, Meta, Google. Roles as AI product managers, applied scientists, trust & safety engineers.
: AI infrastructure, vertical AI solutions. Every industry will be transformed—domain expertise combined with AI skills is valuable.
: Think tanks, government agencies. Policy analysis, research, advising on AI governance.
: You can build AI systems, not just use them
: You understand human behavior and institutions
: You see how components interact (networks, games, emergence)
: You analyze data and build models
: You turn ideas into working code
The field moves fast. Here’s how to stay current:
: Build things. The best way to learn is by doing. Start a blog, contribute to open source, participate in competitions.
Each stage enabled new social forms. We don’t yet know what the intelligence era will bring.
But we know it will reshape:
How we work and create value
How we govern and make decisions
How we learn and discover knowledge
Your generation will navigate this transition.
The tools from this course—networks, game theory, agent-based models, computational thinking, AI agents—will help you:
This course has given you real capabilities:
You can read cutting-edge research papers
in AI, networks, game theory, and computational social science—and actually understand them.
: AI agents with tools, multi-agent coordination, MCP servers, evaluation frameworks.
: Network dynamics, strategic interaction, emergent behavior, collective intelligence.
You can contribute to important problems
: AI safety, mechanism design, human-AI collaboration, AI governance.
The problems we face—climate change, inequality, democratic governance, AI risk—require people who can:
You’re equipped to be those people.
This is the last lecture of the AI module, but not the end of your journey.
The field needs people who are technically skilled, intellectually curious, and thoughtful about implications. People who can build systems that actually work, at scale, safely.
The problems are hard. The stakes are high. And the work is genuinely interesting.
Stay curious. Keep building. Think carefully about impact.
I’m looking forward to seeing what you build, discover, and contribute.
